title: Epistolae Et Decreta
author: Gelasius I
source: Translated by Claude from tmp943.tmp943.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: cum sic te intelligas malum habere affectum , perversumque apostatandi propositum, ut tibi materia prorsus vanitatis illius nulla suppeditet, nec possis astruere quod corde concipis, et ore depromis. Die mihi, cum sæpenumero in Romanis historiis legatur, Livio auctore, saepissime in hac urbc exorta pestilentia infinita hominum millia deperisse; atque eo frequenter ventum, ut vix esset unde illis bellicosis temporibus exercitus potuisset ascribi; illo tempore Deo tuo Februario minime litabatur, an etiam cultus hic omnino nil proderat illo tempore quo Lupercalia celebrabantur?
passages.english: since you may understand that you hold a bad disposition and a perverse purpose of apostasy in such a way that no material at all supplies you for that vanity, and you cannot establish what you conceive in your heart and bring forth with your mouth. Tell me: since it is very often read in the Roman histories, on the authority of Livy, that very frequently, when pestilence arose in this city, countless thousands of people perished, and that things often came to such a point that in those warlike times there was scarcely anyone from whom an army could have been enrolled, was sacrifice not being offered at that time to your god Februarius, or did this worship do no good at all at that time when the Lupercalia were being celebrated?
passages.notes: The opening clause continues the quotation begun in the preceding context ("you have the will to lie, not the skill to invent"); the syntax of "ut tibi materia ... nulla suppeditet" is loose, and the clause is rendered as transmitted. "urbc" read as "urbe". Februarius is the god associated with the February purifications and the Lupercalia. This is the letter of Pope Gelasius I against the Lupercalia, addressed to the senator Andromachus.
